title: Protective human antibodies against a conserved epitope in pre- and postfusion influenza hemagglutinin

venue.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

abstract: Phylogenetically and antigenically distinct influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV) circulate in human populations, causing widespread morbidity. Antibodies (Abs) that bind epitopes conserved in both IAV and IBV hemagglutinins (HAs) could protect against disease by diverse virus subtypes. Only one reported HA Ab, isolated from a combinatorial display library, protects against both IAV and IBV. Thus, there has been so far no information on the likelihood of finding naturally occurring human Abs that bind HAs of diverse IAV subtypes and IBV lineages. We have now recovered from several unrelated human donors five clonal Abs that bind a conserved epitope preferentially exposed in the postfusion conformation of IAV and IVB HA2. These Abs lack neutralizing activity in vitro but in mice provide strong, IgG subtype-dependent protection against lethal IAV and IBV infections. Strategies to elicit similar Abs routinely might contribute to more effective influenza vaccines.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2023 PNAS article has shown clear early scholarly uptake, with 10 citations in OpenAlex, a high citation percentile for its year, and 10 documented downstream reuse instances. Its influence is especially visible in influenza antibody and vaccine research, where it is already being cited by reviews and primary studies that extend the discussion of broadly protective hemagglutinin-directed antibodies.

Full narrative

The article’s main contribution is to the search for human antibodies that recognize a conserved hemagglutinin epitope shared across influenza A and B viruses. That question sits at the center of ongoing efforts to broaden influenza protection, and the paper has quickly become part of that conversation. The citation record shows 10 OpenAlex citations, and the citing literature places the work in a strongly relevant influenza/immunology cluster, including reviews in Immunological Reviews and research articles in virology and vaccine journals.

What stands out most is the speed and shape of the uptake. The downstream reuse graph shows 10 reused-by works, spanning articles, preprints, and reviews, which suggests the paper is being taken up both as evidence and as a conceptual reference point. The balance of citing work types is notable: reviews account for a substantial share of the citing landscape, indicating that the study is already helping to frame broader syntheses of influenza hemagglutinin recognition and broadly protective antibodies.

The citing environment is also international and cross-institutional, with contributions from the United States, Japan, South Korea, and China, and repeated appearances from institutions such as Duke University, the University of Pittsburgh, Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard University, and the National Institute of Infectious Diseases. This pattern is consistent with a paper that is being read across the influenza and antibody research community rather than remaining confined to a single laboratory network.

The broader stewardship context reinforces that trajectory. The work is supported by major biomedical funders, including the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and NIH/NIAID-linked awards, and the article is available in hybrid open access with open instances indexed in repository data. While the public attention record is quiet in the sources provided, the scholarly record is not: the paper has already been incorporated into subsequent influenza antibody research and review literature, indicating meaningful early academic impact.
